nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Indigenous water management practices|Cultural water knowledge_qna_000
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What does TEK stand for in the context of the paragraph?
nodes.answer: TEK stands for Traditional Ecological Knowledge.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Indigenous water management practices|Cultural water knowledge_qna_001
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What is traditional ecological knowledge (TEK), and who are considered the "knowledge holders"?
nodes.answer: Traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) is the accumulated knowledge about the natural world held by local or Indigenous peoples, known as "knowledge holders."

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Indigenous water management practices|Cultural water knowledge_qna_002
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How is Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) related to local ecological knowledge (LEK)?
nodes.answer: TEK of "local people" is synonymous with local ecological knowledge (LEK).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Indigenous water management practices|Cultural water knowledge_qna_003
nodes.question: What is the significance of Indigenous knowledge regarding water in Australia?
nodes.answer: Indigenous knowledge has been developed over thousands of years and is integral to the cultural identity and survival of Indigenous Peoples in Australia, offering valuable insights for water management and planning.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Indigenous water management practices|Cultural water knowledge_qna_004
nodes.question: What role does Indigenous knowledge play in water management in Australia according to the National Cultural Flows Research Project (NCFRP)?
nodes.answer: Indigenous knowledge and stories, acquired through generations, inform the assessment of Aboriginal cultural water values and can complement western science, but there is limited incorporation of these methodologies in water planning due to governmental inaction and dominance of non-Indigenous researchers.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Indigenous water management practices|Cultural water knowledge_qna_005
nodes.question: Why is Indigenous knowledge considered important in water management in Australia?
nodes.answer: Indigenous knowledge is crucial because it is based on generations of observing and understanding territories, providing culturally appropriate methodologies for water management.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean water and sanitation|Indigenous water management practices|Cultural water knowledge_qna_006
nodes.question: What initiative has supported the assessment of Aboriginal cultural water values and recommended changes for cultural flows?
nodes.answer: The National Cultural Flows Research Project (NCFRP) has supported capacity-building and developed robust methodologies for assessing Aboriginal cultural water values, but its take-up by jurisdictions has been limited.
